title: YOUR MOUTH IS TELLING THE TRUTH ABOUT YOUR HEART
paragraphs: YOUR MOUTH IS TELLING THE TRUTH ABOUT YOUR HEART
Understanding “Out of the Abundance of the Heart the Mouth Speaks”—and Why Jesus Was Talking About Something Far Deeper Than Bad Words
There are things you have said that you wish you could pull back into your mouth.
Words spoken in anger.
Words whispered when nobody else was listening.
That cruel sentence you fired at someone you love.
That gossip you dressed up as “concern.”
That sarcastic comment you said was only a joke.
That bitter sentence about the person who hurt you.
That private conversation where a version of you appeared that nobody at church would recognize.
And afterward came the explanation.
“I didn't mean it.”
“I was just angry.”
“I was exhausted.”
“They pushed me too far.”
“That isn't really who I am.”
Maybe.
But Jesus said something uncomfortable enough to make us stop before dismissing our words so quickly.
“For out of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaketh.” — Luke 6:45
The Greek is piercing:
“ἐκ γὰρ περισσεύματος καρδίας λαλεῖ τὸ στόμα αὐτοῦ.”
Ek gar perisseumatos kardias lalei to stoma autou.
In straightforward English:
“For out of the abundance—the overflow—of the heart, his mouth speaks.”
Jesus was not merely giving etiquette lessons.
He was not saying, “Christians should use nicer vocabulary.”
He was revealing something about the human heart.
Your mouth can become a spillway.
And sometimes what spills out tells you what has been accumulating within.
That is why this verse should not merely make us watch our mouths.
It should make us examine our hearts.
Because Jesus did not begin His illustration with speech.
He began with a tree.
“No good tree bears bad fruit, nor again does a bad tree bear good fruit, for each tree is known by its own fruit.”
Then He speaks of treasure.
The good person brings good from the good treasure of the heart, while evil comes from evil treasure.
Then comes the mouth.
In other words, Jesus moves beneath the visible fruit to its hidden source.
Fruit tells you something about the tree.
Words tell you something about the treasury.
The mouth reveals something about the heart.
The Greek word translated “treasure” is θησαυρός — thēsauros.
A treasury.
A storehouse.
Something accumulated and kept.
And suddenly Luke 6:45 becomes painfully personal.
What have you been storing?
Not merely what did you say today.
What have you been depositing into your inner treasury for months?
Resentment?
Envy?
Lust?
Fear?
Self-pity?
Pride?
The need to be admired?
The need to win every argument?
Quiet jealousy toward somebody whose life appears better than yours?
Anger toward the person who wounded you five years ago?
You can hide a treasury for a while.
Then somebody bumps into you hard enough...
and something spills.
A husband explodes at his wife and says, “She made me angry.”
A woman destroys somebody's reputation and says, “I was only telling the truth.”
A believer humiliates another believer online and calls it “defending sound doctrine.”
Someone repeatedly complains about everybody around them but never considers whether discontent has quietly occupied the heart.
Someone makes sexual jokes constantly and insists, “They're only jokes.”
Someone cannot celebrate another person's blessing without immediately finding something wrong with it.
Someone speaks about money constantly.
Someone talks endlessly about themselves.
Someone's conversation repeatedly tears people down.
And Jesus quietly brings us back to the same terrifying possibility:
What if the mouth isn't creating the problem?
What if the mouth is exposing it?
A bottle filled with water does not suddenly produce orange juice because someone shakes it.
Pressure reveals what was already inside.
And life has a way of shaking us.
Traffic.
Bills.
Marriage.
Children.
Rejection.
Church conflict.
Politics.
Social media.
Exhaustion.
Betrayal.
Waiting.
Disappointment.
Someone disrespecting you.
Someone receiving the opportunity you prayed for.
Someone correcting you.
Someone saying “no.”
Someone touching the wound you thought you had buried.
Then suddenly...
the heart spills through the mouth.
This does not mean every careless sentence perfectly defines everything about a person.
Scripture gives room for stumbling. James says, “we all stumble in many ways” and then immediately discusses speech. Peter himself denied Jesus with his mouth and was later restored by Christ.
So Luke 6:45 should never become a weapon for mercilessly diagnosing everyone around us from one sentence.
Jesus' teaching should first become a mirror.
Not binoculars.
Before asking, “What does their mouth reveal about their heart?”
Ask:
“Lord... what does mine reveal about mine?”
That question gets uncomfortable quickly.
Because some of us have learned Christian vocabulary without allowing Christ into certain locked rooms of the heart.
We know when to say, “God bless you.”
We know when to post the verse.
We know when to lift our hands.
We know when to say, “I'll pray for you.”
But Jesus is not impressed by religious vocabulary disconnected from spiritual reality.
Matthew records Jesus using essentially the same truth in an even sharper confrontation:
“How can you speak good, when you are evil? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.” — Matthew 12:34
And shortly afterward Jesus warns that people will give account for their careless words.
That should sober us.
But please don't miss what Jesus is exposing.
The Pharisees' fundamental problem was not that they needed vocabulary training.
They needed hearts that were right before God.
And that distinction changes everything.
Christianity is not primarily Jesus teaching rotten trees how to tape attractive fruit onto their branches.
Jesus came to save sinners.
He came to make us new.
That is why simply trying harder to “speak positively” can never reach the deepest problem.
You can filter vocabulary while resentment remains alive underneath.
You can stop cursing while pride remains untouched.
You can learn church language while secretly despising people.
You can speak softly while manipulating everybody around you.
You can quote Scripture while using Scripture to exalt yourself.
The Gospel goes deeper.
Jesus does not merely want cleaner sentences.
He wants you.
The real you.
The angry you.
The jealous you.
The ashamed you.
The wounded you.
The version nobody sees.
The version that occasionally escapes through your mouth.
And here is where conviction can either drive you toward hiding...
or toward Christ.
Maybe something ugly came out of you recently.
Something so ugly that afterward you sat there thinking:
“Where did that come from?”
Perhaps the better question is:
“Lord, what are You showing me?”
Maybe that explosion revealed resentment you never surrendered.
Maybe the gossip revealed envy.
Maybe the constant criticism revealed pride.
Maybe the cruel joke revealed contempt.
Maybe the defensiveness revealed an identity built upon needing other people's approval.
Maybe the boasting revealed insecurity.
Maybe the endless complaining revealed that circumstances have become more influential over your joy than the promises of God.
Don't waste the revelation.
Don't merely apologize for the sentence and leave the source untouched.
Follow the words upstream.
Back through the mouth.
Back into the heart.
And meet Jesus there.
Because the Christian response to exposed sin is not:
“I need to hide this better.”
It is:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
This is repentance.
Not image management.
Not learning to sound holy.
Not becoming better at suppressing evidence.
Repentance brings what darkness has been protecting into the light of God.
“Lord, this bitterness is mine.”
“This jealousy is mine.”
“This pride is mine.”
“This anger is mine.”
“I cannot blame my spouse anymore.”
“I cannot blame my childhood forever.”
“I cannot blame social media.”
“I cannot blame stress.”
“They may explain the pressure...
but the pressure exposed something inside me.”
And there, at the place where excuses finally die, grace becomes breathtaking.
Because Jesus already knows.
Before your confession, He knows.
Before the mask falls, He knows.
Before everybody discovers what you are ashamed of, Christ knows exactly what resides within the human heart.
And He still went to the cross.
The Gospel is not God discovering good people and rewarding them.
The Gospel is God saving sinners through Jesus Christ.
At Calvary, Jesus did not die for the polished imaginary version of you.
Christ died for sinners.
He bore sin.
He endured judgment.
He shed His blood.
He rose from the grave.
And now forgiveness is not offered because you finally learned how to appear respectable.
Forgiveness is offered through Christ.
That means your ugliest moment does not have to become the final chapter of your story.
Peter's mouth once said:
“I do not know the man.”
Imagine carrying that sentence after the rooster crowed.
Imagine remembering Jesus' face.
Imagine realizing that the mouth that once declared loyalty had just denied Him.
Peter wept bitterly.
But Jesus wasn't finished with Peter.
After the resurrection, Christ restored him.
The mouth that denied Jesus would eventually proclaim Jesus.
That is grace.
Not pretending the denial never happened.
Not calling evil good.
Not minimizing failure.
Grace confronts the scandal...
and then Jesus begins rewriting the story.
Maybe that is exactly what someone reading this needs to hear.
You said terrible things.
You wounded people.
You lied.
You gossiped.
You manipulated.
You cursed.
You denied Christ by the way you lived.
You cannot undo yesterday.
But you can bring yesterday to Jesus.
Confess.
Repent.
Ask forgiveness from the people you wounded where appropriate.
Stop defending what God is confronting.
And believe the Gospel.
Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
There is another beautiful side to Luke 6:45 too.
If the mouth speaks from what fills the heart...
then imagine what happens when the heart is increasingly filled with Christ's truth.
When Scripture begins occupying rooms once inhabited by lies.
When gratitude begins displacing entitlement.
When forgiveness begins replacing revenge.
When humility starts suffocating pride.
When compassion replaces contempt.
When worship becomes louder inside you than worry.
When the Gospel becomes more precious than your reputation.
Something begins changing.
Not perfectly.
Not overnight.
But genuinely.
Your words begin changing because the treasury is changing.
The person who once always needed the last word begins learning silence.
The parent who once screamed begins apologizing.
The husband who once used words as weapons begins using them to build.
The woman who once lived on gossip begins refusing conversations that destroy people.
The believer who once used social media to prove superiority begins asking, “Will this glorify Christ?”
The wounded person who once cursed an enemy begins praying for them.
That is not mere behavior modification.
That is fruit.
And fruit points toward what is happening at the root.
This is why what you repeatedly consume matters.
What you watch.
What you replay.
Whose voices disciple you.
The arguments you feed upon.
The fantasies you entertain.
The grievances you rehearse.
The Scriptures you neglect.
The truth you meditate upon.
The worship you sing when nobody is watching.
Every day, something is entering the treasury.
And eventually...
treasuries spend what they contain.
So perhaps before asking God, “Please control my tongue,” we should also pray:
“Jesus, transform my heart.”
Because you can put a guard at the door...
but Christ wants the house.
You can police the vocabulary...
but Jesus wants the treasury.
You can manage appearances...
but Jesus wants the tree.
And maybe this article has exposed something you have been trying not to name.
Don't run from that conviction.
Run to Christ with it.
If your words have revealed bitterness, confess it.
If they have revealed jealousy, confess it.
If they have revealed lust, confess it.
If they have revealed pride, confess it.
If they have revealed unbelief, fear, hatred, resentment, or unforgiveness, bring it honestly before God.
And if someone else has been wounded by your words, repentance may require more than silently praying about it.
You may need to say:
“I was wrong.”
Not...
“I'm sorry you were offended.”
Not...
“I'm sorry, but you made me angry.”
Simply:
“I sinned against you with my words. Please forgive me.”
There is extraordinary freedom in no longer having to defend the old you.
Because Christ is forming something new.
Not because typing a comment saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes public honesty becomes a small declaration that we are finished pretending.
Let other believers see it.
Let somebody pray.
Let the comment section become more than reactions and emojis. Let it become a place where people stop performing for a moment and admit that we desperately need Jesus.
Somebody who thinks they can never change may need to hear what God's grace has done in you.
Then think of one person.
Not fifty.
One.
The person whose anger is eating them alive.
The friend who loves Jesus but has become bitter.
The husband and wife barely speaking without hurting each other.
The believer whose online words no longer resemble the Christ they profess.
The person carrying shame because of something terrible they said.
Or send this privately.
Not because sharing a Gospel Warrior article earns favor with God. It doesn't.
We are saved by grace, not social-media activity.
But if something points people toward Jesus Christ, repentance, forgiveness, and biblical truth, sharing it can become one simple way of putting truth where someone else may encounter it.
If you want your Facebook presence to glorify God, don't only use it to show people where you went, what you bought, what made you laugh, or what made you angry.
Let some of what you share point people toward Christ.
Someone scrolling tonight may be one sentence away from finally admitting:
“I need Jesus.”
Because there will probably come another moment when somebody presses exactly the wrong button...
and what is inside you wants to spill everywhere.
Come back.
Read Luke 6:43–45 again.
Remember the tree.
Remember the treasury.
Remember the mouth.
Remember the heart.
And remember the Savior who changes sinners from the inside out.
It does not purchase salvation.
It does not make God love you more.
Jesus cannot be bought.
But supporting Gospel work can be one practical expression of generosity when it is done freely, worshipfully, and for God's glory.
Pray.
Send it to someone.

Because supporting Gospel ministry is not only financial. Sometimes you glorify God simply by refusing to keep life-giving truth to yourself and faithfully placing the message of Jesus where another human being can see it.
But above everything else...
don't leave this article merely thinking about your mouth.
Go deeper.
Ask Jesus about your heart.
Because eventually the cup spills.
Eventually the tree produces fruit.
Eventually the treasury opens.
And when it does, the question will not merely be, “What words came out?”
The deeper question will be:
“What had I been storing inside?”
So fill your heart with Christ.
Fill it with His Word.
Fill it with gratitude for the cross.
Fill it with remembrance of mercy.
Fill it with the Gospel until grace begins spilling into conversations where anger once lived.
And when something ugly spills out again—as you continue growing and stumbling—don't hide the evidence.
Take it back to Jesus.
Repent quickly.
Receive His grace.
Make things right.
Keep walking.
Because the most beautiful testimony is not, “I have never failed.”
It is:
“Jesus found me in my failure, forgave me, and He is changing me.”
Your mouth may reveal what has been living in your heart...
but when that heart is surrendered to Jesus, yesterday's overflow does not have to become tomorrow's identity.
